blocks.x: When was that? When did it start? When? Oh, that's been, let me see. George Augustine was a working delegate. Who was that George Augustine? Oh, you know, you lived in St. Edna between Burgundy and Ramport. We used to make meetings there. That's got a big hole there. Yeah. Okay, I'm born. Okay. I'll tell you what you all want. We'll ask you a few questions. Well, that's it. You ask me. I just want to know things like when you were born and where. When I was born? Well, let's wait a little. I think it's working all right.
Go ahead, any time. Just tell us about when you were born.

Yeah, sure. I was born in Louisiana, yeah. I was born on Boilbun, between Scalmers and Cornelius. Oh, yes. And what year was that? 1817. I got my birthday if I can get it. 18... 17. Yes. And your birthday is, when will it be? On the 25th of Monday, 25th of this month. I was born in March. 87 years ago. 87 years ago. No, sir. I'm 87. Me, oh. Yes, that's what I mean. Yeah, that's what you mean. And what was the first kind of music you remember hearing around? Huh? What was the first kind of music you remember hearing in those days? Well, they had me, you're not talking to me, Poesie, you want me to explain to you? Yes. Well, me, I started to play with that bass I made. How old were you then? About 12 years old. 12 years old? Yes, sir. And? And I made the bass, and we had a band together. Guitar, bass, the little bass I made, and a man-lady. Give me. That's right. And how did you say you made the bass out of what? A cheese box. A cheese box. You don't have that in the mood. American cheese, they're all in pieces that come in a big box. Yeah. And I made a little neck, and like I told you, I went and bought some wire, and I made a little bow with wire, got some rosin put on there, and I learned that. You see, that was my first thought. Did they have many of those instruments here in the city then? They had the bass, but I wasn't positioned to buy them. Oh, I see. People had basses. Oh, they had basses, but I was natural at that time, my people didn't have them. They had sufficient, you know, to supply me to get them. When they did, they bought me a good one. When you were young, what kind of music did you hear around town? You know, I mean, before you started playing yourself, what were people playing around? Well, of course, I used to have polka. Polka. Muzuka. Cordrilles. Then, uh, a variety of dances that the white people dance. Varieties, dances. Cordrilles for color. Cordrilles for the colored people, they could dance brightly. That was the outfit. Just like what Cordrilles. Now, the colored people, the colored people, there's four on this side, four on this side. We played the Cordrilles, each of them danced, you know, swing and so on. You understand? Yes. Did they ever play blues then? Blues? Oh. They used to play blues, but they used to play real blues. They don't play no blues now. Right. What was the real blues? Huh? What was it like, the real blues? The real blues is tradition. That's St. Louis blues. It's a little bit of blues. But nobody can come to dig that either, I'll tell you that. The St. Louis blues, that comes a little after, before or after the other blues I'm going to tell you. Is it slow or fast? Slow. Real slow. And I can show you this time, I can dance and show you, I should dance it myself. That's about your hand. Huh? Yeah, that's right. I can do that. Well, knock it out for us. Just give us a beat huh? Yes. Jump On!

Yes. Yes. Now, when you were first starting out, they played those Lancers? Did they play High Society? Oh, they played High Society. That's an old number. They played High Society? Yeah, this was about, maybe, I said 45 years. Do you remember any of the numbers that are saying 70 years ago? 70, oh, man, no, no. 60 years ago. When you first started, what kind of tunes were you playing? Very first when you started to play music. I played on Franklin Street 12 years every night, down the corner of the night, and two, three checks. Played for me from 72. John the Greek. Was that your first job, you said? Oh, no, that was my first job. What was your first job? My first job, I played, I played on a big ankle. That was on Franklin right opposite. Then I got there. I was playing bass so good, the boss, you know, wanted me. Then you spend a dollar on that time, whatever they was playing. Then they wanted me to come over there. Did you still play at that time with a homemade instrument? Sure. That bass you made? No, no, no, no. Oh, no. You bought a bass? Oh, yes. I bought a bass. Oh, yes. You couldn't go around there. You had a real bass by this time. I was a little bass when they were at the 40s, you know? Uh-huh. Six bass and all that. We used to play with six bass. Three pieces of bass. Get all in my little bass there. Get all in my little bass there. Get all in my little bass there. I used to go around and play with different colored people. Ice cream and all that. Young girls, you know? You got no more young girls. That's all you got to read. So anyhow, now. What kind of tunes did you play when you had that first job? Oh, well, I used to play. Walsh, Charlotte, Mazzucca. Well, I don't tell you about the chord reads. Uh-huh. See, that, before you used to play the chord reads, you gave it a different nation. Before you play the chord reads, you play in the hall. You play waltz. You play all dance music, you know what I mean? Or waltz. Then I watch charis and slow drag and all that. But you see, before you get to the chord reads. Now, when you get to the chord reads, when it's time to play the chord reads, you play waltz. Then I feel everybody take this. Take the sheet, you know, as they stand up. So much on this side, so much on this side. Then we play. And we start the chord reads. Then after we... Five parts in the chord reads. Five parts? Yes, sir. You mean all chord reads have five parts? Yes, four. Every one you play has got five parts. Right. And that waltz will make it six. What were the other parts then? Huh? What were the parts? Oh, the parts? Well... First was the introduction, right? The introduction, you know. You just play... Well, the chord reads... You don't dance... They don't dance to waltz already. Well, you're ready for the chord reads. Well, you... I can't sing them to you. But first chord, what you call the chord... Ta-la-la-la-la-la-la-la-la... Ta-la-la-la-la-la-la-la... Now, you see the chord... You... There's a letter over there. You catch your letter, you bring it to you. Then... Or they all do the same thing. Then you... They dance. One... The man dance in the... Let me show you. You can't. I'm going to show you. You see? I suck my shoe up. They got... This is all there. There's the second chord. I was not singing. Well, the middle chord. But just keep on that... That's right. I ain't telling you no lie. Did they play by ear when they played the quadrille? Well, sometimes... Yeah, yeah. The ear. Yes, sir. I know... I play with the best, and I play with the voice. That's the truth before God. I know what happened to the power of state for me. My piece is all that. I know. Tell me, Mr. Gleney, when did you first play slow drags? Slow drags, well, that comes... Slow drags. Well, I tell you about the slow drag proposition. Some of them made... They made slow drag. Be right. Then the other part, then it's like a swing. You see the kind of word for that? Yeah. Yeah, that's my babe. That's one. That's one. All right. Now they got the other shots there, they get a slow drag. When he was coming, I get myself ready, but I didn't know you were surprised. Very young, baby. They all got time, eh? 20. I know. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Good Friday and all that. Playin' out, you got to, if you were only swear I had to lay off, I had to, night off, it was take off. All day and all night. That's right. Now they had twenty-five, twenty-eight, big ankle. Well I can't remember the one that was on Franklin between the Abbeville and the Canal, that's our bank. George Fuqua. Fuqua, yes! That's right. Abbeville, no, that's right. That's what I, no, it couldn't be Franklin. Basin in Abbeville, on that side of the bank. It was the town Lulu White. And then, that, that, uh, big house. I'm going to tell it. They had a mattress on the floor, a pillow, and, uh, and, uh, all them big shots. Man had the money. Anyway, uh, two o'clock where we knocked off, but then we would get some good money there. We'd get, that good money, five dollars a man. Yeah. They said, come play for a dollar and a quarter. No, I didn't. So then they had, so all them big old brothers, you know, got the money. So we go there, we play, and we got the seat on there, and a pillow. I was probably too good, though. But, he was a gay corporate, they called him Jimmy Wright. He'd come down and play, and champagne, all that. They wanted to see how a cause fell off, you know, doing business. Yeah, that's right. Still out, we made the money. And then they'd tip us, too, you know. But Moatma was working at it. You see, many people had a kick. I was young, too, myself, you know. I played one at, uh, Antoine Restaurant. I played a nigger dance there, too. Antoine on St. Louis Street. On St. Louis, between Ryan and Boyle, right? Yeah, I played one there, too. They used to call our band, Gumbu Band. Combo Band. Combo Band. Combo Band? That was a cordial band. Oh. They had, uh, bass, guitar, cordial, drum ron, and the trumpet. Cordial band. German cordial. I used to play flute, you know. That's my first instrument. Two of them. You know what I mean? I used to play flute, uh, after I moved that bass, I used to play flute, a cordial, German cordial. At the same time, that was the time I'm talking about, especially during the war. During the war? I ain't been so long. That's right. That band played by ear? Yes. They had no music. That's good for my time. Were you playing blues with that band? Oh, yeah. The band played by ear. Hey. Hmm? All kinds of different tunes. Yes. All kinds of different numbers, yes. You go there and take a gumbo. No. What's a cow wine? Cow wine? Cow wine? Oh, man. I can clean up with that. I cooked that. Oh, man. Cow wine. I got to tell you all that. Oh, yeah. Buddy Borden at that same time? No. No this is before? After I want to say. After Buddy Borden, Johnson, Johnson Park two bands the Manly Paris band and the Borden band. You see, Mr. Ben is, Albert is there? Yes, he's there. He's a good man. Yes, he's there. So, I said, can I see him? You say yes? Yes, he's a good guy. You know, I said, Albert, I'm not a crew, you know. Albert was going to watch him. Albert was going to watch him. He said, I said, he's going to come in. And he said, he came in. How was you playing tonight? And he's turning the door, right, Mama B? What's the matter? She could say bass, you know. She said, you want to kill my son? That boy ain't got no risk. My God, you want to kill my boy? She's got somebody else who can play bass. She could say bass, you know. Yes. You say, what's the matter? Think I'll play bass, play, and I'll go so much as that. Now he, she's calling, he, she. Oh, yes. He's calling you, she.
What's wrong?

That's he. You, she. 된 stuff Oh, you there? What's your John Robichaud? The violin, the left hand violin? Yes. He dressed so well. Oh, I showed him my friend. Imagine a musician in town, you can tell. That's just my friend there. My father, that's my good friend. Actually, everyone who worked, they know me. I could do nothing. What kind of music they play? John Robichaud's band. What kind of music they play? Oh, they had a band. Up to the minute. He was a musician too. That's what I tell them. I play with the best. That's what I had. But did they play by ear, the Robichaud band? No, no. All the reading? Reading, and they played the proper way too. He was a musician. John, when he was asking for music, I saw Big Gaspar, the drum drum drum player. He told me he was asking for me. I told him I was going to see him. He's got the problems. No. I told him the musician. He's one of them big clubs. I can't call him in that club.
Is the Big Gaspar still around as they live near here? Yeah, but he don't play anymore. He's very sick. About music. About music.
He went to the house there on the island between Roman and Praia. The road right to the church there to restrain between Roman and Praia Johnson on that side of the bank.
He went to double R. I'd like to see him sometime. You can see him. Oh yeah. Did you sick to go to sea? Huh? I don't know. He told me he was very sick.

I went out there with Lawrence. Morato. Morato. Morato. Morato. Yes, he's back. Huh? I know. He stopped playing with Joyce Lewis. I know. He was kind of his heart. Yes. I'm going to learn his part how to play bass. Bill Morato. Is that right? That boy, that old man with the bass player, he beat me. I don't say like somebody, I'm going to learn it. But that boy was a bass player. Yeah, that's just the truth, you know. The truth is the light. Sure.
Absolutely. Sure. What sort of places did you play with Robert Charles' band? Yeah. Yeah.

And Boston Club and Pickwick Club. What's the bass player name? The bass player name is bass. Pickwick, I told you all about that. Oh, love. Was this out near the Yacht Basin where you played? Oh, yeah. It was right across the- West End? No, that's the way you go on the West End, but we get to West End, there's a bridge across there. Bucktown? No, I'm a bridge. Oh, sure, let's come into New Bucktown. I mean, what Bucktown? It was a young bird. Oh, what's he cleaning up there?
There's one place called Tranchino's or something. What? Tranchino's.

Tranchino's. Tranchino's. I played that too already, but I know that too. Hey, Ron played that. Huh? Hey, Ron. Peter on Peter, that's right. Oh, God, I only called him this club. What used to happen out at Millenburg? Huh? What used to happen out at Millenburg? I never was there. What used to happen? Well, they had plenty of camps out there. I played out there regularly. You know, so many job differences. They get picnics at camps out there, paper white, paper colored. And every Sunday, 9 o'clock train, 15 cents round trip. We had a 69 o'clock picnic. So everybody was leaving the fee left for picnics. Two and a half, two and a quarter, two dollars. And all day picnics. You all had all you wanted to eat and drink. Have good time. Did you ever play lawn parties? Lawn parties? Oh, that's me, right? Tell us about it. We never saw one. Huh? Tell us a little. How was a lawn party? A lawn party? What was it like? I never seen one. You never seen one where you were, huh? But you never seen one. I went to a lawn party and that, but they sell you to have a band and drink, eat, dance. That's all. Whiskey, you know. Gombo. You eat Gombo? I love it. I love it. I eat it every day since I came here.
The lawn party was right outdoors. You eat red beans? Oh, yeah.

I can cook them too. Yeah, I don't eat them. I don't eat no kind of beans. No? No. Well, I'll tell you. Used to get a dollar and a half, a dollar and sixty-two dollars, a dime two and a half, a man, you know. It's coming with the people you play for. It was the people you play for. It was the people you play for. It was the people you play for. It was good time. That's called it. They had one of my friends at the camp out there, Lucian. Lucian, what's his name again? What? What? Where's that camp out there? Camp out where?
Oh, at Millenburg.

You always have that in your hospital, you always have anything? You don't know what you're doing. I don't know you don't. I don't believe you know me. But you're not that common man. There's the lawn parties.
Did they dance outdoors? Lawn parties.

Lawn parties. Lawn parties. Is this your party or whatever you got- Outdoors? No, in your house or in the hall, in the way you want to give it. You can give it to your house. You understand? I suppose I feel like giving a party. You get a band and get them out, and a white, you know, and cook, and bombo, and chicken. But didn't you play outdoors sometimes? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Lawn parties. Play in the yard, yes. That's what I'm talking about. Oh, you mean lawn parties. Yes. That's right. I know what you're talking about now. It's good weather though. But it's not bad weather. Well, they give it in the house. You can do it in the house. But it's so hot now. Lawn parties. Yeah. Lawn parties. Man, I feel like that kind of party. I can't tell them the parties I play. I went to Baton Rouge. I played Baton Rouge. I played in, what do you call that place? After you get Baton Rouge, you cross. You had a fair, now they got overpass. What do you call that place? After you-
What? In Alexandria? Oh, I've been there too.

In Shreveport, I guess you went up there. Oh, Shreveport, I had a regular job there. With my- That same big Gasper you're talking about there. We had a good band. Glenn and Gasper, we had a band together. Edgar, you know Edgar? Edgar, he's a violin player in New York. Oh, and yeah. Charlie, Charlie- Well, he had a band with me. Glenn and Glenn, we had a band here when you- Is that so? That's why I used to live at Baton Galveston, Sanan. How long ago was that? Oh, it's been quite a while, but- Been quite a while. You, you, you, man, when you see him tell you- I'm living, now with Glenn, he know. He's four-knows, a policeman. somethin Sugar John. I used to play with Sugar John. He was a dog father. I used to play with him. I said, you ain't a band man. You band that never played in the city of hell. Me. His name is Smith, too. I want to finish Smith's family. Not the same as Frank Smith. Frank Smith. That's his name. He was a cop. I used to work with him, help him. I used to work with him, help him. I used to work with him. I used to play music. He used to play for the guys. Who else did you like? Huh? Who were some of your other favorites? Well, I played with Valtu, violin player. I played with... ...Crimi Brown, Lowe, Julio Valarone, Himal, Pregnant. Who was the best cornet player you ever heard? Well, I'll tell you. In the days we were talking about, the player I was playing with. What do you mean by a ring? No, no. By ear. Well, I'll normally try with a fellow. He read. But he could play by anything, any way you want. Man, Perez is not a good trumpet player, too. Did he play by ear? Who? Perez. He played. Sure he played. Sure he played. He played with me. By ear, though. Yes, yes. That's right. Oh. They...no, no, no, they got the music. They got the music. They got the music. You have to play by ear. But how would you compare Bolden with those people? Bolden? Well, Bolden... Was he as good as them? Who? Bolden, was he as good as... Oh, no! ...Arnold Matoie? No, no, no. No, not for a reason. But he was a good trumpet player. You know he had that. That's right. Camry and Sidon had a bad money. I bet on him. But the man I'm telling you, man who played a race, he said, He said, the musicians was a good trumpet player. But he wasn't a ragtime, you know what I mean? But Bolden. Who was the best ragtime band you ever heard of all? They had an Imperial band. They played good ragtime? Sure. Sure they played good ragtime. Now I think the more rag now, they...it's brave now. It's a boy? It's brave. It's brave. A little one of the ragtime, but we brought the...we used to be a swing...that swing music, just the music that's going today. And if you can't play the blues and all that kind of dances, you're not...that band's no good. But they ain't got that much work. I'm telling you, they ain't got that much work. I sold my bass. You did? How long ago? Oh, but...it was three years ago. I sold them. I didn't play. I don't care about playing.
Tell us about the Teo family. Who was the best member of...it was Papa, Teo, Lorenzo? Who were they? Well, I'm going to tell you.

Louis Teo, that's the oldest one. That's Lorenzo's brother. He lived right down Durban. He was living right down Durban in La Hap. Louis Teo, old Papa, we used to call him Papa. What is his first name? Louis. Louis Teo. Now, Lorenzo, that's his brother. Lorenzo Teo. Now, they had his nephew, Lorenzo's son. He was a clarinet player too. He was in New York. He died in New York, I believe. I used to play with them.
Which one was called Papa Teo?

The oldest one, Lorenzo. He was a cigar maker. Yeah, he was a cigar maker. Papa Teo was Lorenzo Junior's uncle. That's right. That's correct. Under the whole family. Did you know them all? Sure. Who was the best musician in the family? Well, I'm going to tell you, the old man was supposed to be the best. Old man to you. Louis. Yes. I'm telling you. Who was the best man for playing by ear? Lorenzo. Papa, be careful. Who's Lorenzo Junior or the other one? I mean, the old man, the T. or Louis. He play, but he don't care about, play by brand new music. You know? That's the truth. Lorenzo. Well, who was the best man for ear playing? Lorenzo. His brother, Louis' brother. I see. You know what I'm doing? So now, another thing I'm going to tell you. You see, Louis, I used to go home sometimes, old man, I used to go home sometimes, old man, I used to go home sometimes. I said, well, Papa, I got a job there. I want to, you see, when? I said, tomorrow night, I was surprised. Who are you praying for? Who are you praying for? The people, God made you, praying for them lions. He said, only tell you what it means. Who are you praying for? You don't even mean I would not tell you all. You see, when you're praying for white people. Who caught them lions. I said, Lord, everybody. They know. So I tell them, I says, what's the difference? No, they want them lions. Yeah, they want you to make cats on your clown. I can't make cats on my clown. You know what I mean? You want to make all that noise, you know, all that monkey's trying, but you want to play the straight mule. That's what you mean. Yes. Yes, that's right. There ain't no joke about that. One, he was a musician, though, and a good cigar maker, too. One, he was a mole. Now, you all know George Field? Yes. John Bonplay, Dave Chicago. I used to play with him. He used to play with him on Franklin Street, too. Oh, yeah? Yes, indeed. Was he good? Was he good? The boy was a trombone player, man. Sure.
Who were some of the other good trombone players in the old days?

There was, well, Phil was one. They had, uh, Buddy Johnson, he was living in that day, he used to play the superior band. Imperial band. I was playing with him. He had his brother played trombone, too. He had two brothers. Both of them had a barbershop on Tass Street. He died. He used to play with us. His brother died, too.
Oh, that was Yank, Yank Johnson. Yank, Yank. Yeah, that's right.

Oh, yeah. Yank. Yeah, Yank. Do you remember him? You know? Never knew him. Do I know him? Do I know him? You sure do. You sure do, Mr. Glennie. Uh, now wait. Uh, now wait. Uh, you know Joe Petit? Oh, yes. I knew him. I really- He's dead, too. I got to hear him. He's dead. He was living right there. I know where they live in.
Across the Martesian hall. Yeah, exactly.

Uh, now there's another- There's a party called, uh, Yves-On-Moray, between St. Philip and Dumaine, uh, called him, uh, he's a good trombone, but he played more in brass band and I do speak, but he ain't got that much work, no. Uh, uh, Son Handel, you know him? Oh, yeah. He played more brass band, you know. He used to play. He used to play with the country club. That's the- that's the club I was trying to get to. West Virginia is a country club.
Yes, I played that a long time too.
There was a trombonist they tell me about the Baptiste de Lille, I believe. Baptiste de Lille?
Bapt de Lille?
Bapt. Bapt? Wait, wait, look, have you done? I think he lost his mind finally.
He must have been uptown.
Oh yes! He lost his mind?

I believe so, he's dead now. Oh yes, I know Bapt. Sure I know him. Did you know Kid Ori? Huh? Kid Ori? I know him. I can tell you where he comes from, down to the North Parish, Kid Ori. Did you know him? Yes. Did you play with him? If you see Magnifique, you know me helping play. Sure I play with him. When you down here, you know he's got to follow Abimeyash's cousin. He used to play clown, they kind of creeper call him. Cuoco?
Huh?

Cuoco? Cuoco! Tip He was here the other day. He came from California. He used to live on Debonay in the North East for years before he went to California. A big starboard man. He played Bates. Wellman Brog? Wellman Brog? Blown. Big tall old man.
Wasn't Bill Johnson?
Wasn't Bill Johnson. No, wasn't Bill. He was your... Wellman Brog?
Ed Garth.
Paul Foster? I know Foster good.
You're not talking about Foster. Ed Garth. No, he's not big.
No, this was a...
He was in... Is he Cleo?
Yeah, he's from where he lived right there in Durban and...
Is he still playing Bates? He said he stopped. He played guitar too. I don't know. Who did he work with?
But he lived in California. Who did he work with around here? What bands did he play with? Well, you know... He was not much, but he was...
He was all right, Paul.
Well, what was going to tell you all? Well, let's see. Don't be ashamed. Why don't you take me over? Oh. Um... And I wouldn't wait for you too.
Did you tell me one time a few years ago your wife worked at Tom Anderson's too? Did she... I told you what? Did your wife work at Tom Anderson's once? My wife?

Yeah, I was... Maybe it was my wife before my dad. You had so many of them, huh? Yeah, oh man. I had so many of them in my life. If I don't collect them all this world, I would have worked with something. I don't know.
Who were some of the best blues players, you think, around town? The best blues players?
Some really playing blues. Any instruments?
Any instruments?
How many of them did you play? How many of them did you play? Uh... I was forced to fall time, but he's dead too. How many of them did you play? Four... Four... Four...
Ten.
I can't pronounce myself in America. Yeah, I don't know him. No, no, I know you don't know him. Why did you play? Why did you play? Trumpet. And trombone.

segments.title: Interview opening and birth questions
segments.summary: Glenny rambles about a union delegate and street meetings before the interviewers set the recorder going and ask when and where he was born.

segments.title: Birth, the cheese-box bass, and the first music he heard
segments.summary: He says he was born in Louisiana, made a bass from a cheese box at about twelve, and recalls polkas and quadrilles and the old slow blues before St. Louis Blues.

segments.title: Old-time blues of 1904 and who played High Society
segments.summary: He insists the real old blues were played in 1904, and the talk turns to High Society and the clarinetist (Picou) who played it.

segments.title: First jobs on Franklin Street and playing quadrilles by ear
segments.summary: He recounts his first jobs on Franklin Street with a bought bass, the waltz and quadrille dance sets and their five parts, and why playing by ear matters.

segments.chapter: Playing the bass in New Orleans
segments.title: Bowing and picking the bass, Pig Ankle, Lulu White and country dances
segments.summary: He explains bowing and picking the bass, names Johnny Prudence as the first picker, then lists clubs: the Pig Ankle on Franklin, Lulu White's after-hours dances, Antoine's, and country jobs for the Nunez brothers and Delacroix Island.

segments.title: Gumbo band during the Spanish-American War and the Pickwick and Boston clubs
segments.summary: He joined an ear-playing band at about 27 or 28 around the Spanish-American War, called a gumbo band, and played the Pickwick and Boston clubs and with Charles Hippolyte and Piron.

segments.title: Tom Anderson's cabarets and Paul Dominguez
segments.summary: Asked about Storyville cabarets, he says he played for Tom Anderson and for Paul Dominguez, who had cabarets on Rampart-area streets, and describes the bandstands and the crowds.

segments.title: A Mardi Gras job with a bad band and Johnson Park with Bolden
segments.summary: He tells how he took a Mardi Gras pickup job with a rough band and had to lead on bass, then talks of Johnson Park and playing years with a trumpeter who wrote Funky Butt.

segments.title: John Robichaux's band and drummer Big Gaspar
segments.summary: He praises John Robichaux's reading band, and the talk moves to the ailing drummer Big Gaspar and bassist Lawrence Marrero.

segments.title: Boston and Pickwick clubs, Bucktown and Tranchina's
segments.summary: The interviewer asks where he played; he names the Boston and Pickwick clubs, the Bucktown location near the lake and Tranchina's.

segments.title: Millenburg camp picnics and lawn parties
segments.summary: He describes Sunday picnic trains to Milneburg camps, pay of a dollar and a half or so, and lawn parties with gumbo, in the yard or house.

segments.title: Playing in Baton Rouge and Shreveport and with other bandleaders
segments.summary: He mentions jobs in Baton Rouge and a regular job in Shreveport with Big Gaspar, and lists musicians he played with.

segments.title: The Tio family
segments.summary: Asked about the Tios, he sorts out Louis (Papa), his brother Lorenzo and Lorenzo's clarinetist son, and which was the best ear player.

segments.title: Old trombonists: Buddy Johnson, Yank Johnson, Joe Petit, Baptiste de Lille
segments.summary: Asked about trombonists, he names Buddy Johnson and his brothers, Joe Petit, and brass band trombonists. The interviewer also asks about Baptiste de Lille, said to have lost his mind; Glenny says he is dead.

segments.title: Kid Ory and an elusive bass player who moved to California
segments.summary: Glenny says he knew and played with Kid Ory, then the two struggle to identify a big bass player who went to California.

segments.title: Whether his wife worked at Tom Anderson's
segments.summary: He is asked if his wife once worked at Tom Anderson's and jokes about having had many wives.

segments.title: Best blues players
segments.summary: Asked who the best blues players were, he answers confusedly and the recording ends on trumpet and trombone.
